 8.2
  ACCEPTANCE OF AN URBAN AND COMMUNITY FORESTRY OF THE CALIFORNIA
  DEPARTMENT OF FORESTRY AND FIRE PROTECTION GRANT AND
  AUTHORIZATION TO ADVERTISE A REQUEST FOR PROPOSALS FOR
  DEVELOPMENT OF AN URBAN FOREST MANAGEMENT PLAN

  Executive Summary:

  CAL FIRE awarded the City of Lynwood a grant through its Urban and Community
  Forestry Grant Program to prepare an Urban Forest Management Plan and expand the
  City’s tree canopy. Staff requests authorization to release a Request for Proposals (RFP)

City Council Regular Meeting
  2
   for these services. (PW)

  Recommendation:

  Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the attached resolution entitled: A
  Resolution of the City Council of the City of Lynwood Accepting a Grant in the Amount of
  $852,500, from the Urban and Community Forestry Grant Program of the California
  Department of Forestry and Fire Protection and Authorizing the Advertisement of a
  Request for Proposals for the Preparation of an Urban Forest Management Plan,
  Including Urban Forestry Services, Tree Planting and Tree Distribution Services.

 8.3 RATIFICATION OF LETTER OF OPPOSITION FOR SENATE BILL 866 (SB 866)
  Executive Summary:

  The City of Lynwood regularly expresses its support or opposition regarding legislative
  matters that impact the City. As recommended by staff, a letter of opposition for Senate
  Bill 866 (Blakespear) was previously approved and submitted to meet legislative
  deadlines. Opposition letters were due by April 21, 2026, and those submitted by this
  date will be heard in the Senate House Committee. This item is presented for City Council
  ratification of that action and formal inclusion in the public record.

  Senate Bill 866 would require cities that do not receive direct state homelessness funding
  to incorporate extensive homelessness-related reporting requirements into their housing
  elements. While intended to improve transparency, the bill would impose significant
  administrative burdens on cities with limited resources and without access to the funding
  necessary to support such requirements. (CM)

  Recommendation:
  Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Ratify the Mayor’s previously approved and submitted letter of opposition for Senate
  Bill 866 (Blakespear), which was transmitted to meet legislative deadlines; and
  2. Receive and file this report.

 8.4 LOS ANGELES COUNTY FIRE AND AMBULANCE MONTHLY REPORT FOR MARCH
  2026
  Executive Summary:

  This report presents the City Council with its first monthly overview of fire and emergency
  medical services (EMS) response and ambulance transport activity delivered by the Los
  Angeles County Fire Department under contract with the City of Lynwood. Staff is
  establishing this as a consistent monthly reporting structure to keep the City Council
  informed of emergency response activity, system performance, and service demand
  trends.

City Council Regular Meeting
  3
   The report covers key operational metrics including incident types, and ambulance
  transport activity. Staff will compile and present this information monthly to support data-
  informed Council oversight of emergency services, track emerging trends, and evaluate
  system performance over time.

  Staff will continue to compile and present this information on a monthly basis to ensure
  transparency and data-informed decision-making regarding emergency services provided
  to the community. (CM)

  Recommendation:
  Staff recommends the City Council to receive and file the March 2026 Fire and
  Ambulance Monthly Report

 9.  NEW/OLD BUSINESS

 9.1 CITY COUNCIL MEETING SCHEDULE FOR 2026
  Executive Summary:

  This report presents the City Council meeting schedule for the 2026 calendar year and
  requests adoption of a resolution formally establishing those dates and times. Regular
  meetings are held on the first and third Tuesday of each month, with a modified schedule
  in December to accommodate the winter holiday closure in December.

  In addition, staff requests City Council direction on four 2026 Regular Meeting dates that
  conflict with professional conferences or fall during periods identified for additional staff
  work time. Following its review, staff recommends that the City Council adopt the
  resolution to formally establish the meeting dates and times for the 2026 calendar year.
  (CM)

  Recommendation:
  Staff recommends the City Council:

  1. Review and provide direction on the changes to the Regular Meeting dates;
  2. Approve a resolution establishing the meeting dates and times of the City Council
  for calendar year 2026.

 9.2 APPROVAL OF NON-PROFIT APPLICATIONS FOR THE SALE OF SAFE AND SANE
  FIREWORKS
  Executive Summary:

  This report presents four qualified non-profit applicants for approval to operate Safe and
  Sane Fireworks stands from July 1 through July 4, 2026. At its Regular City Council
  Meeting on March 3, 2026, Council authorized the sale of Safe and Sane Fireworks for
  the 2026 season. As of the April 1, 2026 application deadline, the City Clerk’s Office
  received and verified four complete applications. (CC)

City Council Regular Meeting
  4
   Recommendation:
  Staff recommends that the City Council approve the four qualified non-profit organizations
  to operate Safe and Sane Fireworks stands from July 1 through July 4, 2026.

 9.3
  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF LYNWOOD APPROVING
  AN AMENDMENT TO THE 2023-2027 MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
  BETWEEN THE CITY OF LYNWOOD AND THE LYNWOOD EMPLOYEES'
  ASSOCIATION

  Executive Summary:

  This report recommends an amendment to the 2023–2027 Memorandum of
  Understanding (MOU) with the Lynwood Employees’ Association (LEA) to rename the
  City-recognized holiday of Cesar Chavez Day to Farmworker Day.

  The proposed renaming broadens recognition to encompass the collective contributions
  of agricultural workers while continuing to honor the legacy of Cesar Chavez. (HR)

  Recommendation:
  Staff recommends City Council:

  1. Adopt a resolution approving an amendment to amend the 2023–2027
  Memorandum of Understanding between the City of Lynwood and the Lynwood
  Employees’ Association titled, "A Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Lynwood Approving an Amendment to the 2023–27 Memorandum of Understanding
  between the City of Lynwood and the Lynwood Employees' Association," to rename
  the City-recognized holiday of Cesar Chavez Day to Farmworker Day;
  2. Direct staff to update all City policies, administrative documents, calendars, and
  communications to reflect the revised holiday designation; and
  3. Authorize the City Manager or designee to implement this change in a manner
  consistent with applicable laws, memoranda of understanding, and personnel rules.

 Recommendation:

 Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the attached resolution entitled: A Resolution of
 the City Council of the City of Lynwood Accepting a Grant in the Amount of $852,500, from the
 Urban and Community Forestry Grant Program of the California Department of Forestry and
 Fire Protection and Authorizing the Advertisement of a Request for Proposals for the
 Preparation of an Urban Forest Management Plan, Including Urban Forestry Services, Tree
 Planting and Tree Distribution Services.

 Executive Summary:

 CAL FIRE awarded the City of Lynwood a grant through its Urban and Community Forestry
 Grant Program to prepare an Urban Forest Management Plan and expand the City’s tree
 canopy. Staff requests authorization to release a Request for Proposals (RFP) for these
 services. (PW)

 Background:

City Council City Council Regular Meeting
  32
  As part of its efforts to expand the City’s tree canopy, staff partnered with TreePeople to apply
 for a grant through the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE). CAL
 FIRE awarded the City a grant in the amount of $852,500. The grant would fund development
 of an Urban Forest Management Plan (UFMP), planting of 500 trees citywide, and distribution
 of an additional 500 trees to residents.

 The selected contracted firm will conduct a thorough urban forestry assessment covering
 canopy cover locations and percentages, a physical tree inventory, and community input. The
 tree inventory and canopy assessment will directly inform UFMP recommendations to improve
 the immediate and long-term management of the City’s urban forest. The UFMP’s primary
 goal is to improve citywide canopy cover over the long term to combat extreme heat, mitigate
 stormwater runoff and air pollution, and enhance beautification for recreation and public
 health.

 Once the City Council adopts the UFMP, the City will begin implementing its tree planting
 recommendations. Data collection and community feedback will guide tree planting locations,
 species selection, and connectivity corridors. The City will also implement planting through a
 volunteer-led, community-based approach.

 Throughout the UFMP and tree planting processes, the City will educate the community on
 grant activities, tree care, and urban forest management. The City and selected firm will work
 with schools, community groups, and local businesses to involve and engage community
 stakeholders, by hosting a series of local educational workshops, City meetings, and volunteer
 public tree planting events.

 Discussion and Analysis:

 This project represents a transformative effort by the City to develop and implement an Urban
 Forest Management Plan. The City will collect data on existing green infrastructure and gather
 resident-driven feedback on urban forest health. The selected contracted firm will conduct a
 full inventory of all trees in the City and a LiDAR-verified tree canopy analysis, using laser
 scanning (Light Detection and Ranging) to generate precise, 3D measurements of tree height,
 density, and volume. Community surveys and outreach workshops will augment data
 collection to capture residents’ perceptions of the urban environment. Following these
 assessments, the City and firm will develop a UFMP outlining options and recommendations
 for implementation. Staff will review existing City planning documents for alignment with the
 UFMP and address any policy issues that arise. After the City Council approves and adopts
 the UFMP, urban greening will formally begin.

 As outlined in the approved grant, the City will strategically plant at least 500 public trees and
 distribute another 500 to City residents. Local volunteers recruited through neighborhood
 surveys and data collection will support tree planting. After initial community-driven planting
 and tree care events, the City will maintain long-term tree care through a minimum
 establishment period to ensure the sustainability of all green infrastructure installed under this
 project. The City will implement all activities in partnership with TreePeople to support project
 management, equitable community engagement, UFMP research and drafting, tree planting,
 and long-term tree care.

 Recommendation:

  1. Ratify the Mayor’s previously approved and submitted letter of opposition for Senate Bill

  2. Receive and file this report.

 Executive Summary:

 The City of Lynwood regularly expresses its support or opposition regarding legislative matters
 that impact the City. As recommended by staff, a letter of opposition for Senate Bill 866
 (Blakespear) was previously approved and submitted to meet legislative deadlines. Opposition
 letters were due by April 21, 2026, and those submitted by this date will be heard in the
 Senate House Committee. This item is presented for City Council ratification of that action and
 formal inclusion in the public record.

 Senate Bill 866 would require cities that do not receive direct state homelessness funding to
 incorporate extensive homelessness-related reporting requirements into their housing
 elements. While intended to improve transparency, the bill would impose significant
 administrative burdens on cities with limited resources and without access to the funding
 necessary to support such requirements. (CM)

 Background:

City Council City Council Regular Meeting
  39
  The Legislature of the State of California each year proposes legislation addressing housing,
 homelessness, and land use planning. These measures often affect cities’ obligations related
 to housing element compliance and long-term planning.

 The State’s primary homelessness funding program, the Homeless Housing, Assistance, and
 Prevention (HHAP) Program, provides grants to all 58 counties, 44 Continuums of Care, and
 only 14 large cities statewide. Lynwood, like the vast majority of California cities, does not
 receive direct HHAP funding and is therefore not subject to the program’s existing reporting
 framework.

 To receive HHAP funding, grantees must prepare regionally coordinated homelessness action
 plans that include system performance metrics and data reporting requirements. These
 obligations are designed to accompany the receipt of state funding and are conducted within a
 regional framework involving counties and other stakeholders.

 Discussion and Analysis:

 SB 866 would impose HHAP-derived reporting requirements on the very cities the program
 was never designed to fund. Specifically, the bill would require cities that do not receive HHAP
 funding—all but 14 cities statewide, including Lynwood—to incorporate extensive
 homelessness-related reporting requirements into their housing elements. This approach
 effectively penalizes non-recipient cities by mandating compliance with a data infrastructure
 built for and financed through a funding program they do not participate in.

 The bill would replicate HHAP’s system performance metrics. SB 866 would replicate these
 metrics and impose them as standalone requirements on non-recipient cities, obligating them
 to report this data within their housing elements, without any accompanying funding or
 technical support to do so.

 The bill requires detailed reporting on homelessness resources, service coordination efforts,
 and system performance data, including individuals who become homeless after exiting
 institutions such as jails, prisons, and hospitals, and those who become unhoused after
 placement in permanent housing.

 SB 866 also requires cities to report on behavioral health services and funding under the
 Behavioral Health Services Act. However, these services are administered and funded by
 counties, not cities. Because the bill does not apply to counties, it places responsibility on

  cities to report on services outside their control.

 These system performance metrics are currently collected through HHAP’s regional planning
 process because they require coordination with counties, healthcare providers, and other
 stakeholders. Imposing these requirements on individual cities outside of that framework,
 without the corresponding funding, infrastructure, or regional coordination mechanisms,
 creates an unfunded mandate that disproportionately burdens smaller cities like Lynwood that
 are already navigating significant resource constraints. For these reasons, staff recommends
 the City Council ratify the letter of opposition.

Dear Senator Blakespear,

The City of Lynwood must respectfully oppose your SB 866 (Blakespear)
unless amended. SB 866 would require all but 14 cities to add extensive
homelessness reporting requirements to their housing elements, targeting
cities that do not receive state funding to address homelessness.

The state’s flagship homelessness grant program, the Homeless Housing,
Assistance, and Prevention (HHAP) Grant program, allocates funding to all
58 counties, 44 continuums of care, and cities with populations over
300,000. This means that only 14 cities in California are receiving direct state
homelessness funding through HHAP.

To receive HHAP funding, grantees must submit a regionally coordinated
homelessness action plan to the Housing and Community Development
Department that includes specific system performance measures. SB 866
would copy these system performance measures from the HHAP regional
plans and impose them as a separate reporting requirement only on cities
not receiving state funding — forcing them to track these metrics in their
housing elements.

Specifically, SB 866 would require all but 14 cities to provide detailed reports
on available homelessness resources, actions taken to connect individuals
to those resources, and various data points. For example, SB 866 requires

  42
 cities to share information about the number of people who become
homeless after exiting institutional settings, including jails, prisons, and
hospitals, and the number of people who become unhoused after moving
into permanent housing.

SB 866 also requires cities to describe how they are coordinating services
under the Behavioral Health Services Act and identify any available mental
and behavioral health funding. Counties, not cities, provide behavioral
health services in California and receive all the funding to do so. SB 866
does not currently apply to counties because it only applies to local
governments that do not receive HHAP. As a result, SB 866 places the
burden on cities to report on and plan for services beyond their control,
requiring significant reporting on county-led functions within a city's housing
planning document – requirements that cities are not well-positioned to
fulfill.

There is a reason these system performance metrics are currently in the
HHAP regional planning process – because gathering this data requires
collaboration with counties, prisons, hospitals, VAs, and other stakeholders.
These requirements create significant administrative burdens for
communities that already do not receive state financial support to address
homelessness. Nearly all cities lack the infrastructure to collect the data
required by SB 866, making compliance nearly impossible.

Additionally, while HHAP regional plans are updated each year that
funding is available, most communities update their housing elements
every eight years. The City of Lynwood fails to see how collecting this data
every eight years, when much of this information is collected annually
through Continuums of Care point-in-time counts, would help address the
evolving needs of unhoused residents in our community.

The City of Lynwood understands the goal of increasing transparency
around the efforts of smaller cities to address the state’s homelessness crisis.
Currently, cities that do not receive HHAP funding are encouraged to
participate in HHAP regional planning but are not required to do so. The
City of Lynwood is requesting amendments that require smaller cities to
have a seat at the table for the regional planning process. This will
accomplish the same goal, providing transparency into the same system
metrics that SB 866 includes, but through the same regional process already
used by California’s largest cities.

Each year, the Legislature introduces bills that change the rules mid-stream,
significantly complicating cities’ efforts to secure housing element
certification. These multiyear planning efforts are already complex, time-
consuming, and expensive. SB 866 would add a substantial administrative
burden that exceeds the City’s current staffing capacity and available

  43
 resources. Effectively implementing and tracking these new requirements
would likely require resources the City does not have the funding to support.
This challenge is further compounded by the fact that the City of Lynwood
does not receive funding from the Housing and Community Development
Department (HCD) due to its population being under 300,000. As a result,
SB 866 would impose an unfunded, non-reimbursable mandate, placing a
disproportionate burden on smaller cities. For many jurisdictions, including
Lynwood, the difficulty of collecting and reporting this data could further
jeopardize their ability to achieve and maintain a compliant housing
element.

The City of Lynwood urges amendments to SB 866 that ensure consistency
with the existing HHAP regional planning process and do not unfairly target
California’s small cities, which continue to be left out of direct state
homelessness funding.

For these reasons, the City of Lynwood respectfully oppose your SB 866
(Blakespear) unless amended.

 Background:

 emergency response services, including fire suppression, advanced life support (ALS), and
 emergency medical response.

 To enhance Council oversight and provide consistent operational insight, staff is establishing a
 monthly reporting process summarizing fire and EMS activity within the City. This is the first
 report presented under this monthly reporting structure.

 Prior to this reporting structure, staff did not routinely consolidate and present fire and EMS
 performance data to the Council on a standardized monthly basis. Monthly reporting will
 enable staff and the Council to monitor service levels, identify trends, and evaluate emergency
 response performance over time.

 Discussion and Analysis:

 This report covers the monthly fire and EMS statistical summary for March 2026, as compiled
 from data provided by the Los Angeles County Fire Department. The data gives the Council
 with ongoing visibility into emergency response activity and service demand trends.

 During March 2026, the City recorded 117 fire-related incident calls and 538 EMS calls for
 service. Consistent with regional and national trends, EMS incidents represented the majority
 of emergency responses, reflecting the high demand for medical services within the
 community.

 EMS Activity and Patient Outcomes

 The 538 EMS calls included a range of outcomes, including patient transports, non-transport
 incidents, cancellations, and on-scene medical evaluations.

 A portion of these incidents resulted in Advanced Life Support (ALS) transports, where
 paramedics provided care and transported patients to a medical facility. County Fire personnel
 also conducted a small number of interfacility transports were conducted.

 A significant share of EMS responses did not result in transport. Non-transport outcomes
 included:

  Patient refusals of treatment or transport (Against Medical Advice);
  Calls canceled prior to arrival or determined to not require service upon arrival;
  Incidents where the patient could not be located;
  Situations where care was provided on scene without the need for transport; and
  Cases involving deceased individuals or resuscitation efforts that were terminated in
  accordance with established medical protocols.

 These types of outcomes are typical within EMS systems and reflect the role of field personnel
 in assessing patient needs and determining the appropriate level of care.

 Recommendation:

 Staff recommends City Council:

  1. Adopt a resolution approving an amendment to amend the 2023–2027 Memorandum of
  Understanding between the City of Lynwood and the Lynwood Employees’ Association
  titled, "A Resolution of the City Council of the City of Lynwood Approving an Amendment
  to the 2023–27 Memorandum of Understanding between the City of Lynwood and the
  Lynwood Employees' Association," to rename the City-recognized holiday of Cesar
  Chavez Day to Farmworker Day;
  2. Direct staff to update all City policies, administrative documents, calendars, and
  communications to reflect the revised holiday designation; and
  3. Authorize the City Manager or designee to implement this change in a manner
  consistent with applicable laws, memoranda of understanding, and personnel rules.

 Executive Summary:

 This report recommends an amendment to the 2023–2027 Memorandum of Understanding
 (MOU) with the Lynwood Employees’ Association (LEA) to rename the City-recognized
 holiday of Cesar Chavez Day to Farmworker Day.

 The proposed renaming broadens recognition to encompass the collective contributions of
 agricultural workers while continuing to honor the legacy of Cesar Chavez. (HR)

  Background:

 The Lynwood Employees’ Association (LEA) represents non-management employees of the
 City. The City and LEA are parties to a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) governing
 wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment for represented employees for the
 period of July 1, 2023, through June 30, 2027.

 From time to time, amendments to the MOU are necessary to ensure continued alignment with
 operational needs and policy direction. Amendments are permissible under the Meyers-Milias-
 Brown Act (MMBA), subject to approval by the City Council.

 Discussion and Analysis:

 The City Council directed staff to rename the Cesar Chavez Day holiday referenced in the
 MOU to “Farmworker Day,” consistent with recent action taken by the State of California.

 The proposed change is supported by the following considerations:

  1. Broader Recognition of the Workforce: Renaming the holiday expands recognition
  beyond a single historical figure to include the entire farmworker community—past and
  present—whose labor sustains California’s agricultural economy.

  2. Inclusive and Contemporary Framing: This change reflects a more inclusive and
  forward-looking perspective, recognizing that the movement advanced by Cesar Chavez
  continues through today’s workforce and ongoing labor issues.

  3. Alignment with Community Values: The designation “Farmworker Day” may better
  resonate with Lynwood’s community and workforce, reinforcing shared values of equity,
  dignity of labor, and economic contribution.

  4. Educational and Awareness Opportunity: The renaming provides an opportunity to
  expand awareness of:
  Current challenges facing farmworkers
  Their Contributions to regional and national food systems
  Ongoing labor and civil rights issues

  5. Consistency with State Action: The State of California has taken action to formally
  recognize Farmworker Day, reflecting an evolving policy approach toward broader
  workforce recognition. Aligning the City’s holiday designation with the State supports
  consistency and clarity.

 Fiscal Impact:

 There is no fiscal impact associated with the recommended action.

 Executive Summary:

 This report recommends an amendment to the 2023–2027 Memorandum of Understanding
 (MOU) with the Lynwood Employees’ Management Group (LEMG) to rename the City-
 recognized holiday of Cesar Chavez Day to Farmworker Day.

 The proposed renaming broadens recognition to encompass the collective contributions of

 Background:

 The Lynwood Employees’ Management Group (LEMG) represents management employees of
 the City. The City and LEMG are parties to a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)
 governing wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment for represented employees
 for the period of July 1, 2023, through June 30, 2027.

 From time to time, amendments to the MOU are necessary to ensure continued alignment with
 operational needs and policy direction. Amendments are permissible under the Meyers-Milias-
 Brown Act (MMBA), subject to approval by the City Council.

 Discussion and Analysis:

 The City Council directed staff to rename the Cesar Chavez Day holiday referenced in the
 MOU to “Farmworker Day,” consistent with recent action taken by the State of California.

 The proposed change is supported by the following considerations:

  1. Broader Recognition of the Workforce: Renaming the holiday expands recognition
  beyond a single historical figure to include the entire farmworker community—past and
  present—whose labor sustains California’s agricultural economy.

  2. Inclusive and Contemporary Framing: This change reflects a more inclusive and
  forward-looking perspective, recognizing that the movement advanced by Cesar Chavez
  continues through today’s workforce and ongoing labor issues.

  3. Alignment with Community Values: The designation “Farmworker Day” may better
  resonate with Lynwood’s community and workforce, reinforcing shared values of equity,
  dignity of labor, and economic contribution.

  4. Educational and Awareness Opportunity: The renaming provides an opportunity to
  expand awareness of:

  Current challenges facing farmworkers
  Their contributions to regional and national food systems
  Ongoing labor and civil rights issues

  5. Consistency with State Action: The State of California has taken action to formally
  recognize Farmworker Day, reflecting an evolving policy approach toward broader
  workforce recognition. Aligning the City’s holiday designation with the State supports
  consistency and clarity.
